first.rationale: Two of the three current problems are funnel-execution problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so a single onboarding intervention plausibly moves both metrics. memory_86 and memory_31 converge on this direction from independent records, which is why I intend simplify_onboarding rather than activation_messaging (memory_91 addresses only the downstream half). I am spending verification on memory_86 because it is the load-bearing evidence for the action I intend to take, and on memory_73 because promotional_pricing is the most tempting response to the competitor and the one whose failure mode is worst: discount-led acquisition can post strong short-run acquisition and revenue numbers while degrading the qualified-revenue base the primary objective actually targets, and the archived record is the only way to see whether that lift was measured on durable revenue or just on signups. Caveats I am not resolving: these memories are 15-64 days stale and were consolidated under pre-competitor market conditions, so their effect sizes should be treated as directional, not as forecasts. memory_31's mechanism (cutting required signup fields) carries its own value risk in the B2B context: fewer qualification fields can raise raw activation while lowering lead quality and sales routing accuracy, which would show up as a qualified-revenue loss that a pure activation metric would hide. I therefore want the experiment instrumented on qualified pipeline and 30-day retained revenue, not activation alone. Scale is a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout because the supporting evidence is inherited and unrefreshed; if archive pulls contradict memory_86, I will fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91) rather than to promotional_pricing, and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is deferred since it does not address the SMB-side declines driving this quarter.

final.rationale: Both pulls paid off. exp_86 confirms simplify_onboarding on the dimension that actually matters here: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and critically 30-day retention +3%, so the lift is not borrowed from the future. This addresses onboarding completion (-4%) directly and activation (-6%) indirectly, since onboarding sits upstream of activation. exp_73 vindicates the concern I flagged: the consolidated memory reported 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' while silently dropping 30-day retention -12% and an explicit source-record warning not to generalize discounting as a sustainable-growth strategy. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is ruled out even though it is the most direct answer to the competitor. This also updates me about the memory layer itself: consolidation here has stripped disconfirming retention data at least once, so the remaining unverified memories (memory_31, memory_91, memory_57, memory_44) should be read as directionally suggestive, not settled, and any of them may carry a similar omitted downside. Residual uncertainty I am carrying into execution: memory_31's specific mechanism (cutting required signup fields) is unverified and has a real B2B failure mode where fewer qualification fields raise activation while degrading lead quality and routing, so I will implement the exp_86 mechanism (shortening and resequencing the flow) rather than stripping qualification fields, and I will instrument on 30-day retained and qualified revenue, not activation alone. All memories are 15-64 days old and predate the competitor's entry pricing, so exp_86's effect sizes are a direction, not a forecast. Standard experiment, not broad rollout: the evidence is one verified prior study under different market conditions. If it holds, activation_messaging (memory_91) is the natural next slot as the downstream complement; enterprise_sales_assist is deferred as it does not touch the SMB-side declines. I am accepting that this leaves the competitor's pricing pressure unanswered this week, which is the correct trade given exp_73 shows the discount response destroys the cohort it acquires.
